intro: A rabbit outsmarts a bear three harvests in a row. Two brothers tell the same fight over a bike and neither one tells the whole thing. A class reads four lines about a rider in a storm and, the second time through, hears hoofbeats. These are all stories, and each one is built from parts you can learn to see.

In this unit you learn those parts. Characters and what drives them. Setting, plot and the turning point. The lesson hiding under the topic. Who is telling the story and what that teller cannot see. Then poems and plays, which tell stories in their own shapes: lines and stanzas, beats and rhymes, a cast and a script.

By the end, you will be able to take any story, poem or play apart and say what it is made of, who changed, what it means, and how you know. That last part matters most. You will back up every idea with words from the page.
bigQuestion: How is a story built, and how do you find what it really means?

timeline.t: Aesop's fables are told in ancient Greece: short animal stories with a moral at the end.
Greek myths like the story of Icarus explain the world and warn about pride.
Shakespeare writes plays as scripts with a cast, dialogue and scenes, to be spoken on a stage.
Clever-rabbit folktales travel with enslaved Africans to the American South and are told for generations.
Emily Dickinson writes I'm nobody! Who are you? in Amherst and keeps it in a drawer.
Christina Rossetti publishes Sing-Song, with the short poem Who Has Seen the Wind?
Mark Twain's Huckleberry Finn opens with a boy telling his own story in first person.
Robert Louis Stevenson publishes A Child's Garden of Verses, including Windy Nights.
Dickinson's poems are published after her death, and readers meet her for the first time.
Paul Laurence Dunbar comes to Chicago's World's Fair and meets Frederick Douglass.
Dunbar publishes Sympathy, the poem of the caged bird.
You read a story, find its parts and its theme, and prove your ideas from the page.

words.d: a word that tells what a character is like, found by watching what the character does
the reason a character does something
where and when a story takes place
the most tense, turning moment of a plot
the struggle at the center of a story: against another character, nature or oneself
words or events from the text that support an idea
the big idea or lesson about life underneath a story's events
the voice that tells a story, from inside it (first person) or outside it (third person)
a smart guess made from a clue in the text plus what you already know
a group of lines in a poem, set off by blank space
words that make a picture, sound, smell, taste or touch in the reader's mind
instructions in a script that tell actors what to do, not read aloud

test.why: Rabbit's actions show planning and quick thinking.

choices: The main problem and how it was solved
test.why: A summary keeps the main character, problem, key events and ending.

test.why: Quoting the page to support an idea is evidence.
A theme is a sentence about life. A topic is one or two words.

test.q: "We ran until my lungs burned." Which point of view?
test.why: We and my are first-person pronouns.

test.q: Why does Andre's version of the bike story leave out that Mom said yes?
choices: He does not know it, so it is outside his point of view
test.why: A narrator can only tell what he can see from where he stands.

test.why: It is trying to get you to do something.

test.why: The word wait repeats on purpose to build a feeling.

test.why: Slapped the windows lets you hear and feel the rain.

test.why: Dunbar's Sympathy opens with the caged bird.

test.why: Words in parentheses tell the actor what to do.

write.prompt: Pick one character from this unit: Bear, Rabbit, Andre or Jalen. Make a claim about what that character learned, or failed to learn. Support it with at least two pieces of evidence from the story and explain how each one proves your claim.
tips: Claim: say in one sentence what the character learned or did not learn.
Evidence: quote or describe two exact moments from the story, not your feelings about it.
Reasoning: after each piece of evidence, write 'This shows...' and connect it to your claim.
The other side: name one thing a reader might say against your claim, and answer it.
Finish with the theme: what could anyone learn from this character's story?

title: Reading Stories

chapters.title: Story Elements
chapters.bigQuestion: What are the parts every story is built from, and how do you find them?

story.title: Tops and Bottoms
story.kicker: A hungry rabbit, a lazy bear, and one question that turns the whole story around.
paragraphs: Bear owned a big field but hated to work. Rabbit owned nothing but had six hungry kids. One spring Rabbit knocked on Bear's door. "Let me farm your field," he said. "I will do all the work. You just pick which half of each crop you want, the tops or the bottoms." Bear yawned. "Tops," he said, and went back to sleep.

Rabbit planted carrots. He watered, he weeded, he pulled. In the fall he brought Bear a wagon of leafy green tops. Bear got a wagon of leaves. Rabbit's kids got a winter of sweet orange carrots. Bear was angry. "Next year I want the bottoms!"

So Rabbit planted lettuce. In the fall Bear got a wagon of roots and dirt. Rabbit's family ate crisp lettuce all season. Bear roared. "Next year I take the tops AND the bottoms!" Rabbit only nodded, and planted corn.

When Mr. Okafor's class read this tale, he stopped and asked, "Where does the story turn?" Hands went up. Some said the corn. Some said the roar. Then Jada said, "It turns the first time Rabbit asks 'tops or bottoms?' That is when we know he has a plan." Mr. Okafor smiled. She had found the moment the whole story hangs on.

By the third harvest, Bear got a wagon of corn tassels and a wagon of roots. Rabbit's family got the ears of corn, the part in the middle. Bear finally decided to farm the field himself. That, the tale says, is how Bear learned to work.
story.think: Jada said the story turns on a question. Do you agree? Where would you say the turning point is, and why?

lessons.title: Traits Show in Actions
lessons.mainIdea: A character trait is what a character is like, and you find it by watching what the character does and says.
reading: Read this: "Marisol saw the new kid eating alone. She picked up her tray and walked over. 'Can I sit here?' she asked." Nobody says Marisol is kind. But you know it. You saw what she did.

What a person is like is called a *trait*. Kind, brave, lazy, sneaky, and honest are traits. In a story, a writer rarely tells you a trait straight out. Instead the writer shows an *action*. You read the action and name the trait yourself. That is your job as a reader.

Try it with Bear from the tale. He owns a field but will not plant it. He says "tops" and goes back to sleep. Those actions add up. Bear is lazy. Rabbit works all season and thinks ahead. Rabbit is clever and hard-working. Every trait you name should come from something the character actually did.

words.d: a word that tells what a character is like, such as kind, lazy or brave
something a character does in the story

look.title: Two Kids, One Dropped Wallet
look.text: Tomas finds a wallet on the bus floor. He looks around, then slides it into his backpack. Across the aisle, Lena finds a phone. She walks it up to the driver and says, "Somebody lost this."
look.prompt: Name one trait for Tomas and one for Lena. What action did you use for each one?

check.q: How do you usually find out a character's trait?
choices: The writer lists the traits at the start
You watch what the character does and says
check.why: Writers show actions. Readers name the trait from those actions.

check.q: Which word is a trait?
check.why: Honest tells what a person is like. The others name things or days.

check.q: Bear sleeps while Rabbit farms the field. What trait does that action show?
check.why: Bear will not work his own field. That action shows he is lazy.

lessons.title: Why Characters Act
lessons.mainIdea: A motive is the reason a character does something, and feelings often change what a character decides to do.
reading: Why did Rabbit knock on Bear's door? He was not being friendly. He had six hungry kids and no field. That reason is his *motive*. A motive is the reason behind an action. Ask "why did she do that?" and you are looking for a motive.

Feelings drive motives too. A character who is scared may hide or run. A character who is angry may shout something she regrets. Bear roared "tops AND bottoms" because he *felt* cheated. His anger made him greedy, and greed made him easy to trick again.

Writers give clues to feelings without naming them. "Her hands shook. She stared at the floor." Nobody said nervous, but you know. Clues like shaking hands, a tight voice, or a slammed door tell you the feeling. Then the feeling helps you guess the motive for what the character does next.

words.d: the reason a character does something
an emotion such as fear, anger, joy or shame that a character has

look.title: A Motive Hidden in Plain Sight
look.text: Devon offered to walk the neighbor's dog every day for free. His mom was surprised. Devon did not say that the dog lived next door to a girl named Kaya, or that Kaya was usually outside at four o'clock.
look.cite: model text, written for this lesson
look.prompt: What is Devon's real motive? What clue gives it away?

check.q: What is a motive?
choices: The reason a character does something
check.why: A motive is the why behind an action.

check.q: Rabbit knocks on Bear's door. What is his motive?
choices: He wants to be Bear's friend
He wants to sell carrots to Bear
He needs to feed his six kids
check.why: Rabbit has hungry kids and no field. Feeding them is why he acts.

check.q: "Her hands shook. She stared at the floor." What feeling do these clues show?
check.why: Shaking hands and looking down are clues to nervousness or fear.

lessons.title: When a Character Changes
lessons.mainIdea: Many characters are different at the end of a story than at the start, and the change usually comes from what happens to them.
reading: At the start of the tale, Bear will not lift a paw. At the end, he farms his own field. That is a *change*. Bear is not the same bear. Stories about a character who changes are everywhere, because change is what makes a story feel finished.

To track a change, take two snapshots. Snapshot one: what is the character like on page one? Snapshot two: what is he like on the last page? Then ask what happened in between. For Bear, three harvests of leaves and roots taught him a lesson he could not sleep through.

Not every character changes. Rabbit is clever at the start and clever at the end. He is the same. A character who stays the same is called *static*. A character who changes is *dynamic*. When you read, watch for the character who is different at the end. That is usually the one the story is about.

words.d: when a character is different at the end of a story than at the start
a character who stays the same through the whole story
a character who changes because of what happens in the story

look.title: Snapshot One, Snapshot Two
look.text: Page one: Ines refuses to try out for the play. "I will forget every line," she says. Last page: Ines stands on stage in a paper crown, bowing while the crowd claps. Between those pages, her big brother ran lines with her every night for two weeks.
look.prompt: What changed in Ines? What happened in the middle that caused the change?

check.q: Which character in the tale is dynamic?
choices: Rabbit, who is clever all the way through
Bear, who is lazy at first and works at the end
check.why: Bear changes. He starts lazy and ends up farming. That makes him dynamic.

check.q: What does it mean if a character is static?
choices: The character is the main one
check.why: Static means the character does not change during the story.

check.q: What is the best way to track a character's change?
choices: Count how many times the name appears
Skip the middle of the story
Compare the character at the start and at the end
check.why: Two snapshots, start and end, show the change. Then look for the cause in between.

lessons.title: Setting Is Time and Place
lessons.mainIdea: The setting is where and when a story happens, and it shapes what the characters can and cannot do.
reading: "Snow piled against the cabin door. The lamp was almost out of oil." Two sentences, and you already know a lot. It is winter. It is night, or nearly. There is no electricity. This is the *setting*: where and when the story happens.

Setting is not just a background. It changes what can happen. In a snowed-in cabin, a character cannot call for help or run to a store. In a Chicago apartment in July, the problem might be a broken fan and a hot night. Move the same character to a new setting and the story changes with her.

Writers give setting through *details*: the weather, the light, the sounds, the year, the objects around. A story with a horse and a candle is probably set long ago. A story with a bus pass and a phone is set now. Collect the details, and the setting comes into focus.

words.d: where and when a story takes place
a small, specific piece of information, like the weather or an object in the room

look.title: One Sentence, Many Clues
look.text: "Amara pulled her scarf over her nose and waited for the Red Line, stamping her boots on the platform while the wind came off the lake." Read it twice. Look for the season, the city, and the time of day if you can find it.
look.prompt: What is the setting? Which details told you? Is there anything you cannot tell yet?

check.q: What two things does a setting tell you?
check.why: Setting is the place and the time of a story.

check.q: A story has a horse, a candle and a wooden wagon. What can you guess about the setting?
choices: It is set in a big city today
It is set on the moon
It is set in a school
check.why: Candles and wagons are details that point to an earlier time.

check.q: Why does setting matter to the plot?
choices: It tells the reader the ending
It changes what the characters are able to do
check.why: A snowed-in cabin and a city block give characters very different choices.

lessons.title: The Shape of a Plot
lessons.mainIdea: A plot moves from a problem, through events, to a climax, and then to a solution.
reading: Rabbit has no field and hungry kids. That is the *problem*. He makes a deal, plants carrots, plants lettuce, plants corn. Those are the events. Bear roars "tops AND bottoms!" and Rabbit still finds a way. That is the *climax*, the most exciting moment. Bear gives up and farms for himself. That is the *solution*. You just read a whole plot in four sentences.

Almost every story follows this shape. First a problem shows up. Then events pile on and the problem gets harder. Then comes the climax, the turning point where things are most tense. After it, the story slides toward a solution and the ending. Picture a hill: up, up, the top, then down.

Knowing the shape helps you read. When you feel lost in a story, ask: "What is the problem? Has the climax happened yet?" If the character is still struggling, you are on the way up. If things are settling down, you are past the top. This works for a picture book and for a long novel.

words.d: the trouble a character faces that starts the story moving
the most exciting or tense moment of a story, where things turn
how the problem gets settled at the end of a story

look.title: Where the Story Spends Its Time
look.cite: counted for this lesson from the chapter's opening tale
look.prompt: The middle harvests get the most space. Why is the middle of a story usually the longest part?

check.q: In which order do the parts of a plot usually come?
check.why: The problem starts it, events build, the climax turns it, and the solution ends it.

check.q: What is the climax of a story?
check.why: The climax is the top of the hill, where things are most exciting and turn.

check.q: A character is still struggling and the trouble keeps growing. Where are you in the plot?
check.why: Growing trouble means you are on the way up the hill, before the climax.

lessons.title: Three Kinds of Trouble
lessons.mainIdea: A conflict is the struggle in a story, and it can be against another character, against nature, or inside the character's own mind.
reading: Rabbit against Bear. A girl against a blizzard. A boy against his own fear of the diving board. All three are stories, and all three have a struggle at the center. That struggle is the *conflict*. No conflict, no story. If nothing pushes back, there is nothing to read about.

The first kind is character against character. Two people want different things, like Rabbit and Bear both wanting the crop. The second kind is character against nature: a storm, a flood, a long cold winter, a mountain. The character cannot argue with a blizzard. She can only find a way through.

The third kind happens inside. Character against *self* means the fight is in the character's own mind. Should I tell the truth? Can I make myself jump? These stories can feel the most real, because you have had that fight too. Many stories mix kinds. A boy lost in the woods may battle the cold and his own panic at the same time.

words.d: the struggle or problem at the center of a story
a character's own mind and feelings; a conflict against self happens inside

look.title: Sort the Struggles
look.text: Story A: Two sisters fight over who gets the top bunk. Story B: A kayaker's boat flips in cold river water and she has to reach the bank. Story C: Malik knows he broke the window, and nobody saw, and he cannot decide whether to say so.
look.prompt: Which kind of conflict is in each story? Which one do you think would be hardest to live through?

check.q: A hiker is trapped by a snowstorm on a mountain. What kind of conflict is this?
check.why: The hiker is struggling against the weather, which is nature.

check.q: Malik cannot decide whether to admit he broke the window. What kind of conflict is this?
check.why: The fight is inside Malik's own mind. That is character against self.

check.q: Why does a story need a conflict?
choices: Without a struggle there is nothing to read about
check.why: The struggle is what pulls a reader through. Something has to push back.

lessons.title: What Dialogue Shows
lessons.mainIdea: Dialogue is the words characters say, and it reveals who they are and what they want without the writer telling you.
reading: "Give it back." "Make me." Two lines, four words, and you already know these two are fighting and neither one will back down. Words that characters say out loud are *dialogue*. Quotation marks show where the spoken words start and stop.

Dialogue does more than fill space. It shows traits. A character who says "Whatever, I don't care" shows one thing. A character who says "Wait, let me help you carry that" shows another. It shows feelings, too. Short, sharp lines can mean anger. Long, rambling lines can mean nerves.

Dialogue can also move the plot. In the tale, Bear says one word, "tops," and that single word decides the whole first harvest. When you read, slow down at the quotation marks. Ask: what does this line tell me about the person saying it? What does it make happen next?

words.d: the words characters say out loud in a story, shown with quotation marks
the marks " " that go around spoken words

look.title: Same Question, Two Answers
look.text: The coach asked who wanted to take the last shot. "I got it," Ray said, already reaching for the ball. Priya looked at her shoes. "I mean, I could, if nobody else wants to."
look.cite: model text, written for this lesson
look.prompt: What does each line of dialogue show about Ray and about Priya? Point to the exact words.

check.q: What is dialogue?
choices: The place where a story happens
The words characters say out loud
check.why: Dialogue is the characters' spoken words, marked with quotation marks.

check.q: "Wait, let me help you carry that." What trait does this line show?
check.why: Offering to carry something shows the character is helpful.

check.q: How can one line of dialogue move the plot?
choices: It cannot; only actions move the plot
It tells the reader the setting
What a character says can decide what happens next
check.why: Bear's one word, "tops," decided the whole first harvest.

lessons.title: Summarize in a Few Sentences
lessons.mainIdea: A summary retells only the main character, the problem, the big events and the ending, in your own words and in order.
reading: A friend missed the movie and asks what happened. You do not repeat every line. You say who it was about, what went wrong, and how it ended. That short retelling is a *summary*. A good summary is short, in order, and in your own words.

Here is a summary of the chapter's tale: "Rabbit has no field, so he farms Bear's land and lets Bear pick tops or bottoms. Each year Rabbit plants a crop that gives Bear the useless half. After three harvests, Bear gives up and farms for himself." Three sentences. Character, problem, events, ending.

Watch out for two mistakes. One is retelling too much: every carrot, every wagon. The other is giving your *opinion*: "It was funny." A summary is not a review. Leave out what you think and keep only what happened. A test: could someone who never read the story follow your summary? If yes, it works.

words.d: a short retelling of the main parts of a story, in order and in your own words
what you personally think or feel about something

look.title: Three Retellings, Three Lengths
look.cite: counted for this lesson; the tale is the chapter's opening story without the classroom paragraph
look.prompt: The good summary is about one-fifth of the tale. What has to be left out to get it that short, and what has to stay?

check.q: Which of these belongs in a summary?
choices: The main problem and how it was solved
check.why: A summary keeps the main character, problem, big events and ending. Details and opinions stay out.

check.q: "This story was boring but the corn part was okay." What is wrong with this as a summary?
choices: It is in the wrong order
It gives an opinion instead of what happened
check.why: A summary tells what happened. Boring and okay are opinions.

check.q: What is a good test for a summary?
choices: Someone who never read the story could follow it
It is at least a full page
It uses the exact words of the book
check.why: If a stranger can follow it, the summary has the parts that matter.

lessons.title: Prove It From the Page
lessons.mainIdea: When you explain a story, back up your idea with evidence: the exact words or events from the text that show it.
reading: "Bear is lazy." Okay, says your teacher, prove it. You flip to the tale and read: "Bear owned a big field but hated to work." Now it is not just your idea. It is on the page. Words or events from the text that support an idea are called *evidence*.

Evidence turns a guess into an answer. Two students can disagree about a character. The one who can point to the page wins the argument. When you write about a story, use a pattern. Say your idea. Give the evidence. Then explain how the evidence proves the idea.

Try this frame: "I think ___. In the text it says '___.' This shows ___." For example: "I think Rabbit plans ahead. In the text it says he 'only nodded, and planted corn.' This shows he already knew what Bear would ask for." Short, clear, and backed by the page. That is what teachers mean when they say *support* your answer.

words.d: words or events from the text that support an idea about the story
to back up an idea with evidence from the text

look.title: Who Made the Better Case?
look.text: Dani says, "Rabbit is sneaky because I just think he is." Luis says, "Rabbit is sneaky. The text says he 'only nodded, and planted corn' right after Bear asked for both halves. He did not warn Bear at all." The class votes on who made the stronger case.
look.prompt: Who wins the vote, and why? What did Luis do that Dani did not?

check.q: What is text evidence?
choices: Words or events from the story that support an idea
check.why: Evidence is what the page actually says or shows.

check.q: Which sentence uses evidence to support an idea?
choices: Bear is lazy because I think so
Bear is lazy and that is that
Bear is lazy; the text says he 'hated to work'
check.why: Only that answer points to the exact words on the page.

check.q: What is the order of a good evidence answer?
choices: Explain, then idea, then the title
Idea, evidence, then explain how it proves the idea
check.why: I think, the text says, this shows. That is the pattern.

lessons.title: Fables and Their Lessons
lessons.mainIdea: A fable is a very short story, usually with animal characters, that ends with a lesson about how to live.
reading: A hare laughs at a tortoise for being slow. They race. The hare naps halfway, sure he will win. The tortoise keeps plodding and crosses the line first. You know this one. It is a *fable*: a short story, often with animals who talk, that teaches a lesson.

The lesson at the end of a fable is called the *moral*. In the race story, the moral is that steady effort beats careless speed. Many fables are said to come from Aesop. He was a storyteller in ancient Greece more than two thousand years ago. Nobody is sure what Aesop was really like. But the stories with his name traveled all over the world.

Fables work because the animals stand for people. The hare is every show-off who thinks the job is done. The tortoise is every kid who keeps going. When you read a fable, ask two questions. What does each animal stand for? What is the story telling me to do, or not do? Answer those and you have the moral.

words.d: a very short story, often with talking animals, that teaches a lesson
the lesson a fable teaches, often stated at the end

look.title: The Lion and the Mouse
look.text: In one of Aesop's best-known fables, a lion catches a mouse and then lets it go, laughing at the idea that something so small could ever repay him. Later the lion is caught in a hunter's net. The mouse chews through the ropes and sets him free.
look.cite: retold from Aesop's fables (ancient Greece), told here in our own words
look.prompt: What is the moral of this fable? What does the mouse stand for?

check.q: What is a moral?
choices: The first line of a story
check.why: The moral is the lesson at the end, the thing the fable wants you to learn.

check.q: Why do fables often use animals instead of people?
choices: The animals stand for kinds of people
Animals cannot talk in real life
check.why: The hare stands for show-offs and the tortoise for steady workers.

check.q: What is the moral of the tortoise and the hare?
check.why: The tortoise kept going. The hare stopped to nap and lost.

lessons.title: Folktales and Myths Worldwide
lessons.mainIdea: Folktales and myths are old stories passed down by many people, and each culture's stories carry that culture's ideas about how to live.
reading: Nobody wrote the first version of Tops and Bottoms. People told it, and their children told it. It changed a little each time. A story passed down by telling is a *folktale*. Rabbit tales like it were told by enslaved African Americans in the South. Clever-rabbit stories also appear in West Africa, in Native American nations, and in Asia. A small, weak animal who wins by wits shows up almost everywhere.

A *myth* is an old story that explains something big. How did the world begin? Why do seasons change? What are the gods like? In a Greek myth, a boy named Icarus flies on wings of wax and feathers. He flies too near the sun. The wax melts, and he falls. That story explained no weather, but it warned every listener about pride.

Reading stories from many cultures shows you two things. First, people everywhere want the same things: food, safety, fairness, a good laugh at a bully. Second, each culture tells it in its own way, with its own animals, foods and places. When you read a folktale, ask: what did the people who told this care about? The answer is usually the lesson.

words.d: an old story passed down by telling, with no single known author
an old story, often with gods, that explains something about the world
the way of life, beliefs and stories shared by a group of people

look.title: The Same Trick, Two Places
look.text: In one tale, a spider named Anansi from West Africa tricks a bigger animal out of its food by asking a clever question. In another, a rabbit in the American South does almost the same thing to a fox. The animals are different. The trick, and the lesson, are nearly the same.
look.prompt: Why might people in two faraway places tell almost the same story? What did both groups seem to care about?

check.q: How is a folktale different from a story in a new book?
choices: Folktales were passed down by telling, with no single author
check.why: A folktale is handed down by many tellers. A new book has one author.

check.q: What does a myth usually do?
choices: Explains something big, like the seasons or the gods
check.why: Myths explain the world and the gods in story form.

check.q: What lesson does the story of Icarus warn about?
choices: Pride can lead to a fall
check.why: Icarus flew too high because he was proud. The myth warns against that.

review.q: A character gives her lunch to a kid who forgot his. What trait does the action show?
review.why: Sharing food is a generous action.

review.q: The reason a character does something is called the
review.why: A motive is the why behind an action.

review.q: Which part of a plot comes right after the climax?
review.why: After the turning point, the story heads to the solution.

review.q: "Snow piled against the cabin door. The lamp was almost out of oil." What is this mostly telling you?
review.why: Snow, a cabin and a lamp are details of place and time, the setting.

review.q: A boy cannot decide whether to tell the truth. Which conflict is this?
review.why: The struggle is inside his own mind.

review.q: What should a summary leave out?
review.why: A summary keeps what happened and leaves out what you think of it.

review.q: "I think Bear is lazy. The text says he 'hated to work.'" What is the second sentence?
review.why: Quoting the page to back up an idea is evidence.

review.q: Which describes a fable?
choices: A true story about a real person
A long book with many chapters
A story that explains where the sun came from
A short story with animals that teaches a lesson
review.why: Fables are short, often use animals, and end with a moral.

chapters.title: Theme and Point of View
chapters.bigQuestion: How does who tells a story change what it means?

story.title: One Bike, Two Stories
story.kicker: Two brothers, one blue bike, one dented fender, and two versions of what happened on Saturday.
paragraphs: Here is how Andre, who is eleven, tells it. "The bike is mine. Grandpa gave it to me. Jalen took it without asking while I was at practice. When I got home the front fender was dented and he was acting like nothing happened. I yelled because he never asks. He just takes."

Here is how Jalen, who is nine, tells it. "Andre never even rides that bike. It sat in the garage for two weeks. I asked Mom and she said fine, as long as I stayed on our street. A car door opened and I swerved and hit the curb. I was going to tell him. He yelled before I could say a word."

Their mom heard both versions in the kitchen, one brother talking over the other. She held up a hand. "Both of you just told me a true story," she said. "And neither of you told me the whole one." Andre had not known Mom said yes. Jalen had not known the bike was from Grandpa, who died last year.

Ms. Reyes read both versions to her fourth-graders on Monday, without saying which brother was right. Then she asked, "What did Andre know that Jalen did not? What did Jalen know that Andre did not?" The class made two lists on the board. The lists did not match.

"That," said Ms. Reyes, "is point of view. Every storyteller stands in one spot and sees from there. Your job as a reader is to notice where they are standing." Then she asked the harder question: "What is this story really about? Not the bike. Underneath the bike." Somebody in the back said, "Asking." Somebody else said, "Listening first."
story.think: What is the bike story really about, underneath the bike? Which brother's version did you believe more at first, and why?

lessons.title: Theme Is Not Topic
lessons.mainIdea: The topic is what a story is about on the surface; the theme is the big idea or lesson underneath it.
reading: Ask a kid what the bike story is about. "A bike," she says. True, but that is the *topic*: the subject on the surface. Now ask what the story is really about. "Asking before you take." "Listening before you yell." Those are the *theme*: the big idea the story carries underneath.

Here is a quick test. A topic is usually one or two words: friendship, a dog, a race, a bike. A theme is a whole idea you can say in a sentence: "True friends stay when things get hard." "Slow and steady wins." If you can say it as a sentence about life, not just about this story, it is a theme.

Themes are not written on the page. Nobody in the bike story says "the theme is listening." You build the theme from what happens and what the characters learn. That is why two readers can find slightly different themes in one story. Both can be right, as long as each one can point to the events that support it.

words.d: what a story is about on the surface, usually one or two words
the big idea or lesson about life that a story carries underneath the events

look.title: Sort the Sentences
look.text: Here are four sentences: "A lost puppy." "Even small kids can be brave." "Two sisters." "Telling the truth costs less than hiding it." Two of these are topics and two are themes.
look.prompt: Which two are themes? What makes them different from the other two?

check.q: Which is a theme, not a topic?
choices: Asking first saves a lot of trouble
check.why: A theme is an idea about life you can say in a sentence. The others are subjects.

check.q: Where do you find a story's theme?
choices: You build it from what happens and what characters learn
check.why: Themes are not stated. Readers build them from the events.

check.q: "Friendship" is a
check.why: One word naming a subject is a topic. A theme is a full idea about life.

lessons.title: What the Character Learns
lessons.mainIdea: The fastest way to a theme is to ask what the main character learned, and how that lesson could apply to anyone.
reading: At the start, Andre yells first and asks later. At the end, he finds out Mom said yes and that he had the story wrong. What did Andre learn? Get the facts before you blow up. Turn that into a sentence about life and you have a theme: "Ask before you judge."

This works for almost any story. Find the main character. Find what she believes or does at the beginning. Find how she is different at the end. The gap between those two is the *lesson*. The lesson, stated so it fits anyone, is the theme. Sometimes a character does not learn, and the reader is meant to. The hare in the race never says he was wrong. You still know.

One story can hold more than one theme. Jalen's side of the bike story teaches something too: even when you have permission, tell the person it belongs to. Look for the theme by following the character who changed the most. Then check it against the events. If the events *support* it, keep it.

words.d: what a character comes to understand by the end of a story
to back up an idea with events or words from the text

look.title: A Fable With No Moral Printed
look.text: A young crow found a shiny bottle cap and hid it in a tree. He was so busy guarding it that he skipped every meal his mother brought. By winter he was thin and the cap was still shiny. He gave it to his sister and ate.
look.cite: model text, written for this lesson
look.prompt: What did the crow learn? Say the theme in one sentence that could be about a person.

check.q: What is the quickest way to find a theme?
choices: Ask what the main character learned
check.why: The change in the main character points straight at the theme.

check.q: What did Andre learn in the bike story?
choices: Get the facts before you get angry
check.why: Andre yelled before he knew Mom had said yes. He learned to ask first.

check.q: The hare never admits he was wrong. Can the story still have a theme?
choices: No, a character must state it
Yes, the reader learns the lesson even if the hare does not
Yes, but only if there is a moral printed
check.why: Sometimes the reader is the one meant to learn. The events still teach.

lessons.title: Two Stories, One Theme
lessons.mainIdea: Different stories from different times and places can share a theme, and comparing them shows what each one adds.
reading: The bike story and the tortoise-and-hare fable seem to have nothing in common. One has brothers, one has animals. But line them up. In both, someone is too sure of himself. In both, that person ends up wrong. "Being too sure can cost you" fits both stories. That is a *shared theme*.

To *compare* two stories, ask three questions. What theme do they share? How does each one show it? What is different about the way they show it? The fable makes its point in a race, in a page. The bike story makes it in a kitchen, with real feelings. Same idea, different clothes.

Comparing helps you understand the theme better. The fable shows the cost of being too sure: you lose the race. The bike story shows something the fable skips: being too sure can hurt someone you love. Read two stories on one theme and you see it from two sides.

words.d: a big idea that two or more stories carry
to look at two things side by side and find what is the same and what is different

look.title: Line Them Up
look.text: Story one: a girl practices free throws every day for a month and finally makes the team. Story two: an ant carries crumbs all summer while a grasshopper sings, and the ant has food when winter comes. Make two columns: what is the same, what is different.
look.prompt: What theme do both stories share? What does each one show that the other does not?

check.q: What do the bike story and the tortoise-and-hare fable share?
choices: A theme about being too sure
check.why: In both, someone is too sure and ends up wrong.

check.q: Which question helps you compare two stories?
choices: How does each story show the shared theme?
check.why: Comparing means looking at how each story handles the same big idea.

check.q: Why read two stories with the same theme?
choices: You see the idea from two sides
check.why: Each story adds something the other skips.

lessons.title: First Person, Third Person
lessons.mainIdea: In first person a character tells the story using I and me; in third person a narrator outside the story uses he, she and they.
reading: "The bike is mine. Grandpa gave it to me." Who is talking? Andre, about himself. He uses I, me, my. A story told by a character from inside is in *first person*. You are in that character's head, hearing his thoughts, seeing only what he sees.

Now try: "Andre came home and saw the dent. He felt his face get hot." Nobody in the story is talking. A voice from outside tells it, using he, she, they, and names. That is *third person*. The voice telling the story is the *narrator*. A third-person narrator can often see more than one character.

The quickest test is pronouns. I, me, we, my: first person. He, she, they, his, her: third person. Flip through any book and check the first page. Knowing which one you are reading tells you how much to trust the voice. A first-person narrator only knows what she knows, and she can be wrong.

words.d: a story told by a character inside it, using I and me
a story told by a voice outside it, using he, she and they
the voice that tells a story

look.title: A Famous First Line
look.text: You don't know about me without you have read a book by the name of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that ain't no matter.
look.cite: Mark Twain, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, 1884
look.prompt: Which pronouns tell you this is first person? What do you already know about the narrator from the way he talks?

check.q: "I ran to the door and pulled it open." Which point of view is this?
check.why: I is a first-person pronoun. A character inside the story is telling it.

check.q: What is a narrator?
choices: The voice that tells the story
check.why: The narrator is whoever is telling it, inside or outside the story.

check.q: Which pronouns signal third person?
check.why: Third person uses he, she, they and names.

lessons.title: What the Narrator Lets You See
lessons.mainIdea: A narrator's point of view controls what you know, so a reader has to notice what the narrator cannot see or chooses not to say.
reading: When Andre tells it, you never hear that Mom said yes. Not because Andre is lying. He does not know. His *point of view* is the spot he stands in, and from that spot, Mom's kitchen is out of sight. What the narrator does not know, you do not know either, unless you look for gaps.

This means a narrator can be wrong without lying. Andre says, "He never asks. He just takes." That is what it looks like from where Andre stands. From Jalen's spot, he asked the right person. Neither one is making it up. A smart reader asks: what can this narrator see? What might be hidden from him?

Narrators also choose what to tell. Jalen says he swerved for a car door. He does not say how fast he was going. Maybe he was going fast. Maybe he was not. When a narrator skips something, notice the *gap*. The gaps are where the rest of the story lives.

words.d: the spot a narrator stands in, which decides what the narrator can know and tell
something a narrator does not know or leaves out

look.title: How Often Each Brother Says I and Me
look.cite: counted for this lesson from the chapter's opening story
look.prompt: Both brothers talk about themselves and about each other. Does either one say what the other brother was thinking? What does that tell you?

check.q: Why does Andre's version never mention that Mom said yes?
choices: Andre does not know it happened
check.why: From Andre's point of view, that fact is out of sight. He cannot tell what he does not know.

check.q: What is a gap in a story?
choices: Something the narrator leaves out or does not know
check.why: Gaps are what the narrator cannot see or chooses not to say.

check.q: Can a first-person narrator be wrong without lying?
choices: No, being wrong is the same as lying
Yes, the narrator only knows what she can see from her spot
check.why: Andre believed Jalen just took the bike. He was wrong, not lying.

lessons.title: One Event, Two Tellers
lessons.mainIdea: Comparing the same event from two characters shows what each one knows, feels and leaves out, and helps you find the fuller story.
reading: Put the two bike stories side by side. Same Saturday, same dent. Andre: taken without asking. Jalen: Mom said yes. Andre: he was acting like nothing happened. Jalen: I was going to tell him. Every line has a match in the other version, and the matches do not agree.

To compare two accounts, make a chart with three columns: what both say, what only the first says, what only the second says. Both brothers agree there is a dent and that Andre yelled. Only Andre mentions Grandpa. Only Jalen mentions Mom. The middle column is what you can be sure of. The side columns are each teller's *bias*, the way his feelings tilt the story.

Bias is not the same as lying. It just means a person tells the parts that matter most to him. Andre's grief for Grandpa makes the bike matter more. Jalen's feeling of being left out makes the two weeks in the garage matter more. When you read two versions, the fuller story is usually both columns put together.

words.d: one person's telling of what happened
the way a teller's feelings tilt the story toward what matters to that teller

look.title: The Three-Column Chart
look.text: Column one, both say: there was a dent; Andre yelled. Column two, only Andre says: Grandpa gave him the bike; Jalen took it without asking him. Column three, only Jalen says: the bike sat unused for two weeks; Mom gave permission; a car door made him swerve.
look.prompt: Which column would Mom trust most? Which fact from a side column changes the story the most when you learn it?

check.q: What goes in the middle column of a comparison chart?
check.why: The middle column holds what both accounts share. That is what you can be surest of.

check.q: What is bias?
choices: Telling the parts that matter most to you
check.why: Bias is a tilt from feelings, not a lie.

check.q: Which fact appears only in Jalen's account?
choices: Mom said he could ride the bike
check.why: Only Jalen knows Mom gave permission. Andre never heard it.

lessons.title: Why the Author Wrote It
lessons.mainIdea: Authors write to entertain, to inform, or to persuade, and knowing the purpose helps you know how to read.
reading: A joke book, a bus schedule, and a poster that says "Recycle!" were all written on purpose, but not the same purpose. The joke book wants to *entertain*. The schedule wants to *inform*. The poster wants to *persuade* you to do something. Every piece of writing has an author's purpose.

Stories are mostly written to entertain, but not only. A fable entertains and also teaches. A story about a kid who moves to Chicago from another country might entertain, and also help readers understand what that feels like. Ask: what does the writer want to happen inside me when I finish?

Purpose changes how you read. If the purpose is to inform, check the facts. If it is to persuade, watch for one-sided arguments. If it is to entertain, relax and enjoy it, but still ask what it is showing you. The bike story was written to make you think about listening. That is a purpose too.

words.d: to give the reader enjoyment: a laugh, a thrill, a good story
to give the reader facts and information
to try to get the reader to believe or do something

look.title: Three Things on the Fridge
look.text: On the fridge: a comic strip cut from the paper, a note that says "Dentist Tuesday 4:00," and a flyer that says "Vote YES for the new playground, it will make our park safer!"
look.prompt: What is the purpose of each one? How can you tell?

check.q: A poster says, "Turn off the lights and save the planet!" What is its purpose?
check.why: It wants you to do something. That is persuading.

check.q: A bus schedule is written mainly to
check.why: A schedule gives facts. Its purpose is to inform.

check.q: Why does knowing the purpose matter?
choices: It tells you the author's name
It tells you how to read: check facts, watch for one side, or enjoy
check.why: You read a fact sheet, an ad and a story differently.

lessons.title: Making an Inference
lessons.mainIdea: An inference is a smart guess that joins a clue in the text with what you already know.
reading: "Andre had not known Mom said yes." The story never says "Andre felt bad about yelling." But you know he did. How? A clue in the text, plus what you know about people. That is an *inference*: a smart guess built from a clue and your own knowledge.

Here is the formula: clue from the text + what I already know = inference. Clue: a kid comes in soaked, dripping on the floor. What I know: rain soaks people. Inference: it is raining outside. You do this all day without noticing. Reading just asks you to do it on purpose.

An inference is not a wild guess. It has to start from a clue on the page. "Maybe Andre is secretly a robot" is not an inference, because nothing in the story points there. "Andre misses Grandpa" is an inference, because the bike was Grandpa's and Grandpa died last year. The clue is what makes it fair.

words.d: a smart guess made from a clue in the text plus what you already know
a detail in the text that points toward something the text does not say

look.title: Read the Room
look.text: You walk into the kitchen. Two chairs are knocked over. A plate is on the floor in pieces. Your brother is sitting on the counter with the dog on his lap, and the dog's tail is wet with something red.
look.prompt: What do you infer happened? Which clues did you use? What do you know that helped?

check.q: What two things make an inference?
choices: A clue from the text plus what you already know
check.why: Clue plus knowledge equals inference.

check.q: A kid walks in soaked and dripping. What is a fair inference?
check.why: The clue is wet clothes. What you know is that rain soaks people.

check.q: Why is "Andre is secretly a robot" not an inference?
choices: Nothing in the text points to it
check.why: An inference has to start from a real clue on the page.

lessons.title: Backing Up Your Guess
lessons.mainIdea: A good inference comes with its evidence attached: the clue you used and the reasoning that connects it.
reading: In class, Maya says, "Jalen felt guilty." Ms. Reyes asks, "How do you know?" Maya says, "He says 'I was going to tell him.' You only say that when you know you should have said something already." That is an inference with its *evidence* attached. She gave the clue and she explained it.

Use this frame: "I think ___ because the text says ___, and I know that ___." Here is one. I think Jalen felt guilty. The text says he was going to tell Andre. I know people only promise to tell when they feel they owe it. Three parts: the guess, the clue, the *reasoning*.

When you cannot fill in the clue, drop the inference. When you can, you are doing what good readers do: reading what the page says, and also what it means. That is the whole point of reading between the lines. The words are the same for everyone. The meaning is what you build from them.

words.d: the clue from the text that supports an inference
the explanation of how the clue leads to the inference

look.title: The Empty Lunch Bag
look.text: Every day Sam brought a lunch bag to school, and every day at noon he put it, still folded flat, back in his backpack and went out to the yard. On Friday his teacher started leaving a granola bar on his desk.
look.cite: model text, written for this lesson
look.prompt: What do you infer about Sam? What do you infer about the teacher? Give the clue for each.

check.q: Which part is missing from "I think Jalen felt guilty"?
check.why: An inference needs a clue from the text and an explanation attached.

check.q: What is reasoning?
choices: The explanation of how the clue leads to the guess
check.why: Reasoning connects the evidence to the inference.

check.q: You have a guess but cannot find any clue for it. What should you do?
choices: Drop the guess or find a real clue
check.why: An inference without a clue is just a guess. Find one or let it go.

review.q: "Two brothers and a bike" is the story's
review.why: That is the surface subject, the topic. The theme is the idea underneath.

review.q: Which sentence is a theme?
review.why: A theme is an idea about life you can say in a sentence.

review.q: "She grabbed her coat and ran." Which point of view?
review.why: She is a third-person pronoun. A voice outside the story is telling it.

review.q: Why can a first-person narrator be wrong without lying?
choices: The narrator only knows what he can see from his spot
review.why: Andre did not know Mom said yes. He told the truth as he saw it.

review.q: Comparing two accounts, what can you be surest of?
choices: What only the first teller says
review.why: What both accounts share is the firmest ground.

review.q: A flyer says, "Join the library club, it is the best club in school!" Its purpose is to
review.why: It is trying to get you to do something.

review.q: An inference is
choices: a fact stated on the page
a smart guess from a clue plus what you know
review.why: Clue from the text plus your knowledge equals an inference.

review.q: "I think Sam has no lunch because his bag is always flat." Which part is the evidence?
review.why: The flat bag is the clue from the text. The rest is the guess.

chapters.title: Poems and Plays
chapters.bigQuestion: How do poems and plays tell a story differently from a book, and what do you have to do to read them well?

story.title: The Drum Inside the Poem
story.kicker: The first time the class read the poem, it was just words. The second time, they heard hoofbeats.
paragraphs: Mr. Bell put four lines on the board. "Whenever the moon and stars are set, / Whenever the wind is high, / All night long in the dark and wet, / A man goes riding by." He asked Kenji to read them. Kenji read them the way he read everything: fast, flat, done. "Okay," said Mr. Bell. "Now we read it again. This time, listen for the drum."

"What drum?" said Kenji. Mr. Bell did not answer. He tapped the desk. Tap, TAP, tap, TAP. Then he read the first line, slow, letting his voice land hard on some words and light on others. "Whenever the MOON and STARS are SET." A few kids started tapping too. By the third line, the whole room was doing it.

"That," said Mr. Bell, "is a horse." The poem is about a rider who gallops past in the storm every night, and the poet built the sound of hooves right into the words. Robert Louis Stevenson wrote it more than a hundred years ago for a book of poems for children. He was a sick boy who spent a lot of nights awake, listening to the wind.

Kenji read the lines a third time, tapping as he went. This time he slowed down at "dark and wet" and sped up at "riding by." It sounded like a story. It sounded a little scary. "I didn't get that the first time," he said. "Nobody does," said Mr. Bell. "A poem is not finished until you hear it."

Then Mr. Bell handed out a one-page play with two parts, a rider and a child at a window. "Same night, same storm," he said. "But this time you are going to say the words out loud and be the people. That is the other thing we do with words on a page: we stand up and become them."
story.think: What changed between Kenji's first reading and his third? Why do you think a poem might need to be heard, not just seen?

lessons.title: Lines and Stanzas
lessons.mainIdea: A poem is built from lines, and lines are grouped into stanzas; where a line breaks is a choice the poet made.
reading: Look at a page of a story. The words run to the edge and wrap around. Now look at a poem. The words stop early, on purpose, and start again on the next line. Each row of a poem is a *line*. The poet decides where every line ends. That is the first thing that makes a poem look like a poem.

Lines are grouped into *stanzas*. A stanza is a chunk of lines with a space before and after it. It works a little like a paragraph. Each stanza often holds one picture or one step of the idea. When you reach the white space, pause. Something is about to shift.

Try this short poem, written for this lesson: "The bus is late. / The rain is cold. / My shoes are wet. / My socks are old." Four lines, one stanza. Each line is one small complaint, and the line breaks make you feel them one at a time. Written as a sentence, they would blur together. Broken into lines, each one lands.

words.d: one row of words in a poem, ending where the poet chose to stop
a group of lines in a poem, set off by blank space, like a paragraph

look.title: Same Words, Two Shapes
look.text: Version one: "The bus is late, the rain is cold, my shoes are wet, my socks are old." Version two: "The bus is late. / The rain is cold. / My shoes are wet. / My socks are old." Read each one out loud.
look.prompt: Which version sounds more tired and fed up? What do the line breaks do to the way you read it?

check.q: What is a stanza?
choices: A group of lines in a poem set off by blank space
The last line of a poem
check.why: A stanza is a chunk of lines, a bit like a paragraph.

check.q: Who decides where a poem's line ends?
check.why: Line breaks are the poet's choice, not an accident of the page.

check.q: What should you do when you reach the white space between stanzas?
check.why: Each stanza often holds one picture or step. The space is a signal to pause.

lessons.title: Rhythm and Rhyme
lessons.mainIdea: Rhythm is the beat made by stressed and unstressed syllables, and rhyme is matching sounds at the ends of lines.
reading: Say your own name and listen. One part is louder. KEN-ji. Ma-RI-a. Every word has beats, and some beats are stressed, or louder. A poet lines up stressed beats in a pattern, and that pattern is *rhythm*. It is the drum Mr. Bell's class heard: "whenEVer the MOON and STARS are SET."

*Rhyme* is a different tool. It is a match of sounds at the ends of lines. Set and wet. High and by. Cold and old. Rhyme makes lines stick together and makes a poem easy to remember. That is why songs and jump-rope chants rhyme. Not every poem rhymes, but when one does, you can hear the ends of the lines click shut.

You can find rhythm by tapping and rhyme by listening to the last word of each line. Try it on this: "I lost my hat, / I found my hat, / It's on the cat." Tap: the beat is steady, bump-BUMP-bump-BUMP. Listen: hat, hat, cat. Rhythm and rhyme together are why the poem sounds like a little song.

words.d: the beat of a poem, made by the pattern of louder and softer syllables
matching sounds at the ends of words, like set and wet
said louder or harder than the beats around it

look.title: Syllables in Four Lines of Windy Nights
rows: Whenever the moon and stars are set,
All night long in the dark and wet,
look.cite: counted for this lesson; lines by Robert Louis Stevenson, A Child's Garden of Verses, 1885
look.prompt: The lines get shorter toward the end of the stanza. Read them aloud. What does the short last line do to the sound of the rider?

check.q: What makes a poem's rhythm?
choices: The pattern of stressed and unstressed beats
check.why: Rhythm is the beat, made by which syllables get stressed.

check.q: Which pair rhymes?
check.why: High and by end with the same sound.

check.q: Why do so many songs and chants rhyme?
choices: Rhyme makes lines stick together and easy to remember
check.why: Matching sounds help words stay in your head.

lessons.title: Saying It Again
lessons.mainIdea: Poets repeat words, lines and sounds on purpose, and the repetition tells you what matters most.
reading: "Whenever the moon and stars are set, / Whenever the wind is high." Two lines in a row start with the same word. That is not a mistake. It is *repetition*, saying something again on purpose. Repeating "whenever" makes the storm feel like it comes again and again, every night.

Repetition works like a drumbeat you cannot ignore. Repeat a word and the reader notices it. Repeat a whole line and it becomes a *refrain*, like the chorus of a song. Songs use refrains because the part you hear most is the part you remember. Poems do the same thing.

Here is a tiny poem written for this lesson: "Wait for the bus. / Wait for the bell. / Wait for the light. / Wait for the tell-tale click of the door." The word wait comes four times. You feel the waiting. When a poet repeats something, ask what feeling the repeat is building. That feeling is usually close to the heart of the poem.

words.d: using the same word, line or sound more than once on purpose
a line or group of lines repeated in a poem or song, like a chorus

look.title: One Word, Over and Over
look.text: Wait for the bus. / Wait for the bell. / Wait for the light. / Wait for the tell-tale click of the door.
look.cite: model poem, written for this lesson
look.prompt: Which word repeats? What feeling does the repetition build, and why is the last line longer?

check.q: What is repetition in a poem?
choices: A mistake the poet forgot to fix
Using the same word or line again on purpose
A rhyme at the end of a line
check.why: Poets repeat on purpose, to make you notice and feel the words.

check.q: A whole line that repeats in a poem or song is called a
check.why: A refrain is a repeated line, like a chorus.

check.q: In the model poem, what does repeating "wait" make you feel?
choices: The long slow feeling of waiting
check.why: Four waits in a row build the feeling of waiting itself.

lessons.title: Reading a Poem Aloud
lessons.mainIdea: A poem is meant to be heard, so read it aloud slowly, following the punctuation, not just the line ends.
reading: Kenji's first reading was fast and flat, and the poem stayed dead on the board. His third reading was slow, with taps, and the poem woke up. Reading a poem out loud is not a test of speed. It is how you find the sound the poet built into it.

Three rules help. First, slow down. A poem packs a lot into few words, so give each word room. Second, follow the *punctuation*, not the line ends. If a line has no period or comma at the end, keep going into the next line without a big stop. Third, let your voice rise and fall with the rhythm. Tap it out if that helps.

Fourth, and this one matters: read it more than once. The first time, just get the words. The second time, listen for the beat. The third time, try to sound like the poem feels: spooky, sleepy, excited, sad. Every time you *perform* a poem this way, you understand it better. That is not cheating. That is reading.

words.d: marks like periods and commas that tell a reader where to pause or stop
to read or act something out loud for others, with feeling

look.title: Where Does the Voice Stop?
look.text: Two lines from a poem written for this lesson: "The kite pulled hard against my hand / and then let go." There is no mark at the end of the first line. Read it with a full stop after hand. Now read it straight through, pausing only at the period.
look.prompt: Which reading matches what a kite does? Why should you follow the punctuation and not just the line end?

check.q: A line of a poem ends with no punctuation. What should your voice do?
choices: Keep moving into the next line
check.why: Follow the punctuation. No mark means no big stop.

check.q: Why read a poem more than once?
choices: Because the first reading is always wrong
Each reading finds something new: words, then beat, then feeling
check.why: First the words, then the rhythm, then the feeling. Each pass adds something.

check.q: What was wrong with Kenji's first reading?
choices: It was fast and flat, so the sound never showed
check.why: Fast and flat hides the drum. Slow and tapped brings it out.

lessons.title: Pictures Made of Words
lessons.mainIdea: Imagery is language that makes a picture, sound, smell, taste or touch in the reader's mind, using the five senses.
reading: "All night long in the dark and wet." You cannot see the storm, but you can feel it: dark, wet, cold, long. Words that make you see, hear, smell, taste or touch something are *imagery*. A poet uses imagery so you do not just read about the storm. You stand in it.

Imagery works through the five *senses*. Sight: a red kite against gray clouds. Sound: the slap of rain on the windows. Smell: wet dog. Taste: a mouthful of salt water. Touch: the scratch of a wool sweater. Good poets pick the one detail that puts you there. "It was a nice day" is not imagery. "The sidewalk burned through my flip-flops" is.

When you read a poem, hunt for the senses. Underline the words you can see. Circle the ones you can hear or feel. Then ask what the poet wanted you to notice most. A poem about summer that talks only about heat is telling you something. A poem about winter that mentions the smell of soup is telling you something else.

words.d: words that create a picture, sound, smell, taste or touch in the reader's mind
sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch: the five ways we take in the world

look.title: Wind You Cannot See
look.text: Who has seen the wind? / Neither I nor you: / But when the leaves hang trembling, / The wind is passing through.
look.prompt: The wind cannot be seen. Which word lets you see it anyway? Which sense is the poet using?

check.q: Which sentence uses imagery?
choices: The sidewalk burned through my flip-flops
check.why: Burned through my flip-flops makes you feel the heat. The others just tell.

check.q: What are the five senses?
check.why: Imagery reaches the reader through those five senses.

check.q: "The leaves hang trembling." Which sense does this reach?
check.why: You see the leaves shaking. That is how the poem shows the wind.

lessons.title: Words That Sound Like Sounds
lessons.mainIdea: Some words sound like the noise they name, and poets use them to put sound directly into a line.
reading: Buzz. Crash. Drip. Hiss. Say them out loud. Each one sounds like the thing it means. A word that imitates a sound is a *sound word*. The long name for it is onomatopoeia, which is hard to spell and fun to say. You already use sound words all the time: a dog goes woof, a clock goes tick.

Poets love sound words because they do two jobs at once. They name the sound and they make it. "The bacon sizzled" tells you and lets you hear it. In the wait poem, "the tell-tale click of the door" ends on a sound you can almost hear. Click is short and sharp, like a real latch.

Sound is also built into softer tricks. Repeating the same first sound in a row of words, like "slow, slippery, slush," is called *alliteration*. It makes the line feel slick. A poet chooses sounds the way a cook chooses spices. Read the poem aloud and notice which sounds keep coming back. They are there for a reason.

words.d: a word that imitates a real noise, like buzz or crash; also called onomatopoeia
the same beginning sound repeated in words close together, like slow slippery slush

look.title: The Kitchen at Seven
look.text: A poem written for this lesson: "Sizzle of eggs, / clatter of plates, / the fridge door thunk, / the kettle's rising whistle, / and under it all / the hum." Read it aloud. Some words are noises. Some just describe.
look.prompt: Which words are sound words? Which one comes closest to the real noise? Which sound would you add?

check.q: Which word is a sound word?
check.why: Hiss sounds like the noise it names.

check.q: What is alliteration?
choices: The same beginning sound in words close together
A rhyme at the end of lines
check.why: Slow, slippery, slush all start with the same sound.

check.q: Why do poets use sound words?
choices: They are the only words allowed
They name a sound and make the sound at the same time
check.why: Sizzle tells you about bacon and lets you hear it.

lessons.title: Dickinson and Rossetti
lessons.mainIdea: Emily Dickinson and Christina Rossetti wrote short poems with plain words that still carry big feelings when you read them closely.
reading: "I'm nobody! Who are you? / Are you nobody, too?" That is how one of Emily Dickinson's most famous poems begins. Dickinson lived in Amherst, Massachusetts, in the 1800s. She rarely left her house and published almost nothing while she was alive. After she died in 1886, her family found hundreds of poems in her room.

Look at those two lines closely. Nobody is usually an insult. Dickinson turns it into a secret handshake: are you nobody too? Then we can be nobodies together. The words are tiny. The idea, that you do not have to be famous to matter, is not tiny at all. Reading closely means slowing down until you see that.

Christina Rossetti, an English poet born in 1830, wrote the wind poem you read earlier. Her poems for children are short and sound like songs. Both poets prove something worth knowing: a poem does not need long words or long lines. It needs the right words. When you read them, ask what each small word is doing. Usually it is doing a lot.

words.d: reading slowly and carefully, noticing what each word is doing
to print writing so other people can read it

look.title: Nobody Meets Nobody
look.text: I'm nobody! Who are you? / Are you nobody, too?
look.cite: Emily Dickinson, opening lines of a poem written about 1861 and published in 1891
look.prompt: Why might the speaker be glad to meet another nobody? Is being nobody a bad thing in this poem?

check.q: What was unusual about Emily Dickinson's life as a poet?
choices: She published almost nothing while alive
check.why: Most of her poems were found after her death in 1886.

check.q: In "I'm nobody! Who are you?" how does Dickinson use the word nobody?
choices: As an insult to the reader
As a name for a monster
As a friendly secret shared with the reader
check.why: She turns nobody into a bond: we can be nobodies together.

check.q: What do Dickinson and Rossetti show about poems?
choices: Short, plain words can carry big ideas
check.why: Both used small words and short lines to say large things.

lessons.title: Stevenson and Dunbar
lessons.mainIdea: Robert Louis Stevenson wrote poems from a child's eye, and Paul Laurence Dunbar wrote poems full of music and feeling about freedom.
reading: "How do you like to go up in a swing, / Up in the air so blue?" Robert Louis Stevenson wrote that. He was born in Scotland in 1850. He also wrote the adventure book Treasure Island. As a boy he was sick a lot and spent long days in bed. Many of his poems for children are about what a kid sees from a bed, a window or a swing.

Paul Laurence Dunbar was born in Dayton, Ohio, in 1872. His parents had been *enslaved*. He wrote poems while working as an elevator operator. He became one of the first Black American poets read all over the country. In 1893 he came to Chicago for the World's Fair. There he met Frederick Douglass.

Dunbar's poem Sympathy begins, "I know why the caged bird sings, ah me, / When his wing is bruised and his bosom sore." A bird in a cage *stands for* a person who is not free. Reading Dunbar closely means asking what the bird stands for. He died young, at 33. His lines are still read aloud today.

words.d: represents; a caged bird stands for a person who is not free
forced to work for someone as their property, with no freedom

look.title: The Caged Bird
look.text: I know why the caged bird sings, ah me, / When his wing is bruised and his bosom sore.
look.cite: Paul Laurence Dunbar, opening of Sympathy, 1899
look.prompt: What might the cage stand for? Why does the bird sing when it is hurt?

check.q: What are many of Stevenson's children's poems about?
choices: What a child sees from a bed, window or swing
check.why: Stevenson was sick as a boy and wrote from a child's eye view.

check.q: In Dunbar's Sympathy, the caged bird stands for
choices: a person who is not free
check.why: The bird in a cage represents someone denied freedom.

check.q: Which fact about Dunbar is true?
choices: His parents had been enslaved and he became a famous poet
check.why: Dunbar, born in Ohio to formerly enslaved parents, became a nationally read poet.

lessons.title: Reading a Script
lessons.mainIdea: A play is written as a script with a cast list, lines of dialogue, stage directions and scenes, and each part has a job.
reading: A play does not look like a story. It looks like this. CAST: RIDER, CHILD. SCENE 1: A window, night. Wind. CHILD: (pressing her face to the glass) Who is out there? RIDER: (from far off) Only me, and the storm. The words a character says come after the character's name. Everything else is instructions.

The list of characters at the top is the *cast*. The words after a name are that character's lines, the dialogue. The words in parentheses, like (pressing her face to the glass), are *stage directions*. They tell actors what to do, not what to say. You never read them out loud.

A play is cut into *scenes*. A new scene usually means a new place or a new time. "SCENE 2: The same window, morning." When you read a play alone, picture the stage. When you read it with others, each person takes a part. The story only exists when someone speaks the lines. That is the strange, great thing about a play.

words.d: the list of characters in a play
instructions in a script, often in parentheses, telling actors what to do
one part of a play, usually set in one place and time

look.title: A Very Short Scene
look.text: SCENE 1. A kitchen, morning. MOM: (holding up a dented fender) Which one of you wants to go first? ANDRE: (pointing) Him. JALEN: (at the same time, pointing) Him. MOM: (sitting down) Great. This should be quick.
look.cite: model script, written for this lesson
look.prompt: Which words would you say aloud? Which would you only do? How do the stage directions make the scene funny?

check.q: What are stage directions?
choices: Instructions telling actors what to do, not read aloud
check.why: Words in parentheses tell actors what to do. They are not spoken.

check.q: What does a new scene usually mean?
check.why: Scenes divide a play by where and when it happens.

check.q: Where do you find a character's spoken lines in a script?
check.why: The character's name comes first, then the words that character says.

lessons.title: Reader's Theater
lessons.mainIdea: In reader's theater you read a script aloud with a group, using your voice to become the character, with no costumes or memorizing needed.
reading: Mr. Bell's class did not build a set or sew costumes. They pulled chairs into a half circle, took parts, and read the storm play out loud. That is *reader's theater*. You keep the script in your hands. Your voice does the acting. It is the easiest way to perform a play, and one of the best ways to get better at reading.

Your voice has tools. Volume: loud for the rider shouting over the wind, soft for the child at the window. Speed: fast when scared, slow when sleepy. *Tone*: the feeling in your voice, angry or kind or teasing. Read your line to yourself first, decide what the character feels, then say it that way.

Two habits make it work. Read your part more than once before the group starts. And listen to the others, so you come in on time. Kids who do reader's theater often read faster and smoother afterward, because they have practiced the same lines until the words feel like their own. Reading out loud with feeling is practice that does not feel like practice.

words.d: performing a play by reading the script aloud in a group, with voices instead of costumes
the feeling in a voice, such as angry, kind, scared or teasing

look.title: One Line, Four Ways
look.text: The line is: "Only me, and the storm." Say it as a tired old rider. Say it as a ghost. Say it as someone trying not to scare a small child. Say it as someone trying very hard to scare a small child.
look.prompt: What did you change each time: volume, speed or tone? Which version fits the poem best?

check.q: What do you use to act in reader's theater?
choices: Your voice, with the script in your hands
check.why: Reader's theater is reading aloud with feeling. No costumes or memorizing.

check.q: What is tone?
check.why: Tone is the emotion your voice carries: angry, kind, scared.

check.q: Why does reader's theater help students read better?
choices: They practice the same lines until the words feel like their own
There is no reading in it
check.why: Repeated reading with feeling builds speed and smoothness.

lessons.title: Poem, Story, Play
lessons.mainIdea: A poem, a story and a play can all tell about the same thing, but each form gives the reader something different.
reading: A rider gallops through a storm at night. Stevenson made it a poem: four short lines, a drumbeat, one picture. Mr. Bell's play made it two voices, a child and a rider, talking across the wind. A story could make it a whole chapter: who the rider is, where he is going, why the child cannot sleep. Same night, three *forms*.

Each form has strengths. A poem is short and musical, so it gives you a feeling fast. A story gives you time: characters, setting, a plot with a problem and a solution. A play gives you voices and puts you in the room. When you *compare* forms, ask: what can this one do that the others cannot?

Try it yourself. Take any small moment, like the first snow of the year in Illinois. As a poem it might be six lines about the hush. As a story it might be a kid who wakes up, sees white, and races to find her boots. As a play it might be two kids at a bus stop arguing about whether school will close. All three are true. Each one shows a different side.

words.d: the shape a piece of writing takes, such as a poem, a story or a play
to look at two or more things side by side and find what is the same and what is different

look.title: First Snow, Three Ways
look.text: Version one, a poem: six short lines about the hush when snow falls on a Chicago street at night. Version two, a story: a girl wakes up, sees white out the window, and tears the house apart looking for her boots. Version three, a play: two kids at a bus stop arguing about whether school will close.
look.prompt: Which version would you rather read? Which would you rather write? What does each form do that the others cannot?

check.q: What does a play give a reader that a poem usually does not?
choices: Different characters' voices speaking to each other
check.why: A play is built from dialogue between characters.

check.q: Which form usually gives the most time for characters, setting and plot?
check.why: A story has room to build characters and a full plot.

check.q: What does comparing three forms about the same thing show you?
choices: Each form shows a different side
check.why: Same moment, three forms, three different strengths.

review.q: A group of lines in a poem set off by blank space is a
review.why: A stanza is the poem's version of a paragraph.

review.q: What made the class hear hoofbeats in Stevenson's poem?
review.why: The pattern of stressed syllables makes the galloping sound.

review.q: A line that repeats in a poem, like a chorus, is a
review.why: A refrain is a repeated line.

review.q: "The sidewalk burned through my flip-flops." This is an example of
review.why: It makes you feel the heat through touch. That is imagery.

review.q: Which word sounds like the noise it names?
review.why: Crash is a sound word.

review.q: Which poet wrote the lines about the caged bird?
review.why: Dunbar's Sympathy opens with the caged bird.

review.q: In a script, what are the words in parentheses?
review.why: Parentheses hold instructions for the actors.

review.q: What do you need for reader's theater?
review.why: Reader's theater is reading a script aloud with feeling.
